bosses.name: Phisher Phil
bosses.tag: Hooks you with fake bank links
bosses.intro: Tap my link! It looks just like your bank. What could go wrong?
bosses.beat: My fake link is dead. Nobody tapped it!

qs.q: An SMS says: "Your SBI account is blocked. Update PAN now: sbi-update-kyc.top/login". What do you do?
o: Tap the link and log in quickly
Reply STOP to the sender
Ignore the link and open the bank's own app to check
qs.why: Real banks do not send KYC links like this, and the address is not the bank's real site. Check only in the official app or at the branch.

qs.q: Which web address is most likely the real HDFC Bank site?
o: hdfc-bank-secure.xyz
hdfcbank.com.login-help.in
hdfcbank.com
qs.why: The real owner is the name just before the last ending. In the third address that is login-help.in, so hdfcbank.com is only a decoy at the front.

qs.q: A message says "Claim your ₹5,000 refund" with a short link (bit.ly/x1y2). Safest move?
o: Open it on a spare phone
Do not open it. Check refunds inside the shopping app itself
Open it, but type nothing
qs.why: A short link hides where it really goes, and just opening a page can be risky. Real refunds show up in the official app or your bank statement.

qs.q: A web page shows a padlock (HTTPS). Does that prove the site is genuine?
o: No. Scam sites can have a padlock too
Yes. The padlock means it is safe
Yes, if the padlock is green
qs.why: The padlock only means the connection is encrypted. It says nothing about who owns the site, so always read the address carefully.

qs.q: You typed your password on a fake page by mistake. What is the first step?
o: Wait and see if anything happens
Change that password at once on the real site and turn on 2-step login
Delete the SMS and forget it
qs.why: Act fast: change the password, switch on 2-step verification and check recent activity. If money moved, call 1930 straight away.

bosses.name: Vishing Vera
bosses.tag: Phones you pretending to be the bank
bosses.intro: Hello sir, this is your bank. Your KYC expires today. Please share the OTP.
bosses.beat: The line went dead. You hung up on me!

qs.q: A caller says, "I am from your bank, your KYC expires today. Tell me the OTP just sent." What now?
o: Share only the last 3 digits
Hang up and call the number printed on your bank card
Share the OTP, since it is the bank
qs.why: Banks never ask for an OTP or PIN. Even part of an OTP helps a scammer, so end the call and use the official number.

qs.q: The caller ID shows your bank's real name. Can you trust the call?
o: Yes. Caller ID cannot be faked
No. Caller names and numbers can be faked
Yes, if the number starts with 1800
qs.why: Scammers can fake what shows on your screen. Hang up and call the number on your card or in the bank's app.

qs.q: She already knows your name and the last 4 digits of your card. What does that prove?
o: Nothing. Leaked data is easy to buy or steal
That she must work for the bank
That she is from the RBI
qs.why: Scammers use leaked details to sound real. Knowing facts about you is not proof of who is calling.

qs.q: "Your debit card will be blocked in 30 minutes!" What is the real warning sign?
o: That the caller speaks English
The caller's polite voice
The tight deadline meant to scare you
qs.why: Fear plus a deadline is a pressure trick. Slow down and check with the bank yourself.

qs.q: What is the safest way to check a call that says it is from your bank?
o: Call back the number the caller gave you
Press 1 as the caller says
Hang up and call the number on the back of your card
qs.why: A number you find yourself on your card or in the app is trustworthy. A number the caller gives you may lead straight back to the scammer.

bosses.name: Digital Arrest Dan
bosses.tag: Says you are "arrested" on a video call
bosses.intro: You are under digital arrest! Stay on camera and pay the fine now!
bosses.beat: Case closed. There was never any arrest!

qs.q: On a video call a "police officer" says you are under "digital arrest" and must stay on camera. What is the truth?
o: There is no "digital arrest" in Indian law. It is a scam
It is legal for 24 hours only
It is legal, so you must obey
qs.why: Police, CBI and other agencies do not arrest anyone over a video call. Hang up and tell a family member.

qs.q: He says your parcel had drugs and you must pay a "deposit" to clear your name. Real agencies would...
o: Accept deposits by UPI to settle cases
Accept deposits only at night
Never ask for money over a call to close a case
qs.why: No genuine agency collects money by phone or UPI to close a case. Demands like this are the scam.

qs.q: He says, "This is a secret investigation. Do not tell anyone." Best reaction?
o: Keep it secret as ordered
Hang up and tell a family member or trusted adult right away
Keep the video call on for longer
qs.why: Secrecy keeps victims alone and scared. Telling someone you trust breaks the trick.

qs.q: The caller sends an official-looking notice with a police logo and stamp on WhatsApp. It proves...
o: That it is genuine because it is a PDF
Nothing. Logos and stamps are easy to copy
That the notice is genuine because of the stamp
qs.why: Anyone can copy a logo, a stamp or a signature. Genuine notices do not arrive on WhatsApp with a demand to pay.

qs.q: You already paid ₹20,000 after such a call. What is the first move?
o: Call 1930 and your bank immediately, then file at cybercrime.gov.in
Pay more to "cancel" the case
Wait for them to refund you
qs.why: The first hour matters most. Call 1930, tell your bank, and keep every screenshot and transaction ID.

bosses.name: QR Quincy
bosses.tag: Makes you PAY when you think you RECEIVE
bosses.intro: Scan my QR to receive your money! (Shh, it only works one way...)
bosses.beat: My code is scrambled. You can't be tricked!

qs.q: A "buyer" says, "Scan this QR and enter your PIN to receive ₹3,000." What really happens?
o: You receive ₹3,000
Nothing happens
₹3,000 leaves your account
qs.why: A UPI PIN approves money going OUT. You never need a PIN or a QR scan to receive money.

qs.q: When do you actually enter your UPI PIN?
o: To look at a QR code
To receive money
To send money, or to check your balance
qs.why: A PIN approves a payment or shows your balance. It is never needed to receive money.

qs.q: While you sell a phone, a stranger sends a "collect request". Should you approve it to get paid?
o: Yes, that is how you get paid
No. Approving a collect request pays THEM
Yes, but only for half the amount
qs.why: A collect request asks you to send money. Genuine buyers only need your UPI ID.

qs.q: At a petrol pump you scan the pump's own QR, the app shows the pump's name, and you pay ₹500. Is the PIN normal here?
o: No. You must never enter a PIN
Yes. You chose to pay and the name matches
Only if the amount is zero
qs.why: This is a normal payment you started yourself to a known business. Always check the name and amount before the PIN.

qs.q: A sticker with a QR code is pasted over a shop's original QR. Smart step?
o: Scan it. All QR codes are the same
Pay double just in case
Check the name shown in your app and ask the shopkeeper before paying
qs.why: Scammers paste their own QR over a real one. The name your app shows before you pay is your safety check.

bosses.name: OTP Ogre
bosses.tag: Grabs the codes that unlock your money
bosses.intro: Just read me that little code. I promise I will not open the vault. Mwahaha!
bosses.beat: My vault key is broken. Nobody shared a code!

qs.q: Who is allowed to ask you for your OTP or UPI PIN?
o: The police
Bank staff
Nobody. Never share them with anyone
qs.why: OTPs and PINs are only for you. Banks, NPCI, police and delivery staff never need you to read them out over a call or chat.

qs.q: You get an OTP you did not ask for, then a caller asks you to read it out "to cancel the payment". You...
o: Read it out to cancel
Share it only with a polite caller
Never share it. Someone may be trying to get into your account
qs.why: An OTP you did not request means someone is trying to access your account. Sharing it lets them in.

qs.q: An SMS says "OTP for ₹9,800 to XYZ. Do not share." You bought nothing. What next?
o: Reply with the OTP to cancel it
Tap the link in the SMS to cancel
Do not share it, and check your bank app. Call the bank on its official number if worried
qs.why: The OTP is useless unless someone gives it away. Check your account safely and never tap a link in such a message.

qs.q: A friend messages: "Send me the 6-digit code you just got, I typed your number by mistake." What is likely happening?
o: A friend made a harmless typing mistake
Someone is trying to take over your WhatsApp. Do not share the code
A normal WhatsApp update
qs.why: The code lets them log in as you. Even if the message looks like it is from a friend, never forward a verification code.

qs.q: A website says, "Enter your ATM PIN to claim cashback." Verdict?
o: Scam. An ATM PIN is only for ATMs and card machines
Fine if the site looks nice
Fine if the site has HTTPS
qs.why: No genuine cashback needs your card PIN. A nice design or a padlock proves nothing.

bosses.name: Remote Rex
bosses.tag: Wants to see and control your phone
bosses.intro: Install this little app so I can help. I will just watch... everything.
bosses.beat: Connection lost. Your screen is yours again!

qs.q: A "bank support agent" asks you to install AnyDesk to fix your app. Smart reply?
o: Install it, since it is support
Refuse. Remote apps let strangers see your screen and OTPs
Install it but switch off the screen
qs.why: Remote-access apps give a stranger full view and control. Real banks never ask you to install them.

qs.q: You already installed the app and shared the 9-digit code. First thing to do?
o: Wait for the agent to finish
Turn on airplane mode, uninstall the app, call your bank from another phone
Keep it but change the wallpaper
qs.why: Cut the connection first, then remove the app and tell your bank. Change passwords and your PIN only once the phone is clean.

qs.q: Why are screen-sharing apps dangerous during a scam call?
o: They use up your storage
The caller can see your screen, read OTPs and move money
They slow the phone down
qs.why: Everything on your screen is visible to them, including OTPs, notifications and banking apps.

qs.q: Which apps should you never install just because a stranger asks?
o: A calculator
AnyDesk, TeamViewer and other "quick support" apps
A calendar
qs.why: Remote-access apps are the scammer's favourite tool. Install apps only from the official app store, and only when you decided to.

qs.q: Is it safe to open your banking app while a stranger is watching through screen share?
o: Yes, with a strong PIN
No. They can see everything you type or see
Yes, if you cover the camera
qs.why: Screen sharing shows them your screen, including what you type. End the share before doing anything.

bosses.name: Lottery Lucy
bosses.tag: Says you won something you never entered
bosses.intro: Congratulations! You won a million! Just pay a tiny fee...
bosses.beat: No prize, no fee. The jackpot was fake!

qs.q: SMS: "You won ₹25 lakh in a lottery! Pay ₹5,000 processing fee to claim." What do you do?
o: Pay it, because the prize is bigger
Pay half now and half later
Ignore it. You cannot win a contest you never entered, and real prizes need no fee
qs.why: Asking you to pay first is the giveaway. Genuine prizes never need an advance fee.

qs.q: Which is a red flag in a prize message?
o: It arrives as a text message
It says congratulations
You must pay a fee or tax first to receive it
qs.why: Money going out before a "prize" comes in is the classic trap.

qs.q: A "spin and win" link arrives on WhatsApp from an unknown number. Safe?
o: Yes, free spins are harmless
No. Open the real app yourself instead of the link
Yes, if friends forwarded it
qs.why: Links in forwarded messages can lead to fake sites that steal data or money.

qs.q: A "cashback" collect request pops up on your UPI app. To receive the cashback you should...
o: Decline it. Cashback never needs you to approve a payment request
Approve it and enter your PIN
Approve it but with a small amount
qs.why: Approving a request sends money out. Real cashback is credited without you doing anything.

qs.q: A cousin forwards "win a free phone, share with 10 friends". What is it most likely?
o: A fair giveaway
A chain scam that spreads links and collects data
A government scheme
qs.why: Free-phone chains are a classic way to spread dangerous links. Do not forward them.

bosses.name: Job Joker
bosses.tag: Pays you a little, then takes a lot
bosses.intro: Easy job! Like videos, earn money! Just deposit a tiny amount first...
bosses.beat: Fired! No more fake jobs from me!

qs.q: A Telegram job says: "Like videos, earn ₹500 per task. Deposit ₹1,000 first to unlock tasks." Verdict?
o: Fine if others in the group earned money
A small risk, worth a try
A task scam. Real jobs do not make you pay to work
qs.why: Paying to work is the clue. The "others" in the group are often part of the scam.

qs.q: They pay a small ₹150 first, then ask for ₹10,000 to "upgrade". This pattern is...
o: Normal trust building
A bonus for good work
Bait to make you pay much more
qs.why: A tiny early payout makes it feel real. The big "upgrade" payment is the real aim.

qs.q: A recruiter asks for a "security deposit" for your laptop before you start. Real employers...
o: Often take deposits by UPI
Do not charge you to be hired
Only charge freshers
qs.why: Genuine employers pay you. Fees, deposits and "training charges" before a job are a scam sign.

qs.q: A work-from-home job offers ₹60,000 a month and needs no interview. Best step?
o: Check the company on its official website and well-known job sites. Do not pay to apply
Send your Aadhaar and bank details at once
Share the job link with friends
qs.why: Offers that are too easy and too good need checking. Never send ID or bank details before you verify the employer.

qs.q: You lost money in a task scam. Which proof should you keep?
o: Nothing, delete the chats
Screenshots, chats, phone numbers and transaction IDs
Only the company logo
qs.why: Evidence helps 1930 and the police act. Never delete chats or payment records.

bosses.name: Invest Ivan
bosses.intro: Guaranteed 30% every month! Join my secret trading group now!
bosses.beat: My chart crashed. Sure profits do not exist!

qs.q: A WhatsApp group promises "guaranteed 30% a month" on a trading app. Verdict?
o: OK if the group has 500 members
Guaranteed high returns do not exist. It is a scam
Great, join it
qs.why: No genuine investment can promise a fixed high profit. Big groups are easy to fake.

qs.q: How can you check if an investment adviser is genuine?
o: Look for the name in SEBI's registered list on sebi.gov.in
Count their followers
Ask them if they are registered
qs.why: Registered advisers are listed by SEBI. Followers, screenshots and promises prove nothing.

qs.q: The app shows big profits, but to withdraw you must pay "tax" first. What now?
o: Pay half the tax
Stop paying. The profits on screen are fake
Pay the tax to get your money
qs.why: Fake apps show pretend gains and keep asking for more "fees". Real tax is not paid to a stranger's account.

qs.q: A famous person in a video endorses an investment platform. What should you think?
o: Share it with family
Videos and voices can be faked with AI. Check on official channels
It must be real, since it is a celebrity
qs.why: Deepfake endorsements are used to sell scams. Verify through the person's or company's official page.

qs.q: Which rule is the safest?
o: High returns mean high safety
If it promises sure profits or tells you to hurry, walk away
Join only secret groups
qs.why: Pressure and guarantees are the two classic signs of an investment scam.

bosses.name: Loan-Shark Lenny
bosses.intro: Instant loan! No documents! Just let me see all your contacts and photos.
bosses.beat: Loan cancelled. I could not scare you!

qs.q: A loan app wants access to your contacts and photos. What does that suggest?
o: A risk. Some apps misuse them to threaten people. Refuse or uninstall
A rule from the RBI
Normal security
qs.why: Genuine lenders do not need your contacts or photos. Some fake apps use them to shame and blackmail borrowers.

qs.q: A lender asks you to pay a "processing fee" to a personal UPI ID before sending the loan. This is...
o: A tax
Normal practice
A scam sign. Genuine lenders do not ask you to pay upfront into personal accounts
qs.why: Paying first to someone's personal account is how loan frauds work.

qs.q: After a tiny loan, they threaten to send your photo to your contacts. First move?
o: Pay whatever they ask
Delete your phone number
Do not panic or pay more. Save evidence, tell a trusted adult and report to 1930
qs.why: Threats are meant to scare you. Keep screenshots, tell someone you trust and report it.

qs.q: Which habit lowers loan-app risk the most?
o: Share your Aadhaar on chat first
Use any app with 5-star ads
Borrow only from banks and lenders regulated by the RBI, and install apps from official stores
qs.why: Check that the lender is a regulated one before sharing anything.

qs.q: An app says "Loan approved in 2 minutes, no documents." The best thought is...
o: Too easy is suspicious. Verify the lender first
Send the OTP to speed it up
Wow, perfect
qs.why: Real lending involves checks. A promise of instant, no-check money is bait.

bosses.name: SIM-Swap Sid
bosses.tag: Steals your phone number to read your OTPs
bosses.intro: I have copied your number. All your OTPs are mine now.
bosses.beat: Signal restored. Your number is yours again!

qs.q: Your phone suddenly has no signal for hours and strange SIM-change messages arrive. What might be happening?
o: The phone battery is old
The network is just slow
A possible SIM swap. Contact your mobile operator and bank at once
qs.why: With a SIM swap, a criminal moves your number to their SIM to catch your OTPs. Act quickly.

qs.q: A caller asks you to share a code to "upgrade your SIM to 5G". Verdict?
o: Scam. SIM-upgrade calls are used to steal numbers
Do it, it is free
Fine, if the caller sounds friendly
qs.why: Never share codes for a SIM upgrade. Your operator will not ask for that over a call.

qs.q: Which government portal lets you see the mobile connections registered on your ID and report ones you do not use?
o: upi.gov.in
npci.org.in/sim
sancharsaathi.gov.in
qs.why: The Department of Telecommunications runs Sanchar Saathi, which also lets you report suspected fraud calls and messages.

qs.q: Why do scammers want control of your mobile number?
o: To raise your bill
To send you photos
To receive your OTPs and reset your passwords
qs.why: Many accounts send OTPs to your number. Whoever has the number can get them.

qs.q: Which habit protects you best from number theft?
o: Do not hand out ID copies casually, and tell your operator if your signal vanishes
Post your SIM number online
Use one PIN for everything
qs.why: Fewer copies of your ID and a quick report when your signal drops make it harder to misuse your number.

bosses.name: Marketplace Mal
bosses.tag: Pretends to buy or sell on classifieds
bosses.intro: I am an army officer! Scan my QR and the money comes to you... honest!
bosses.beat: Listing removed. No more fake deals!

qs.q: A "buyer" says he is an army officer and sends a QR: "Scan it and enter your PIN to receive money."
o: Refuse. A PIN only sends money out
Ask him to pay double
Scan it to be polite
qs.why: Anyone can claim to be an officer. Receiving money never needs a PIN or QR scan.

qs.q: A seller asks ₹500 in advance "to hold the bike" and sends photos. You have not met. Smart move?
o: Pay, since it is small
Do not pay in advance. Meet and check the item first
Pay now and visit later
qs.why: Advance payments to strangers are the most common marketplace trick.

qs.q: A buyer sends a "payment sent" screenshot, but your own bank app shows no credit. What does that mean?
o: Money will come later, so hand over the goods
Do not hand over anything. Screenshots can be fake
Hand over half now
qs.why: Only your own bank or UPI app, or your bank SMS, can confirm money arrived.

qs.q: A "courier" asks the seller to pay a delivery fee through a link. Smart?
o: Pay it twice to be safe
No. Genuine buyers and couriers do not need fees from the seller through links
Pay it, it is small
qs.why: A fee link is how money and card details get stolen.

qs.q: Where is it safest to meet a stranger who wants to buy your item?
o: Their home
A quiet lane at night
A busy public place in daytime, with someone with you
qs.why: Public places and company protect you from both scams and worse.

bosses.name: Deepfake Dee
bosses.tag: Copies a loved one's face or voice
bosses.intro: Mummy, it is me! Send money now! (Do I sound like him? I copied his voice.)
bosses.beat: My mask slipped. Family code word wins!

qs.q: A call in your uncle's voice says he is in trouble and needs ₹20,000 now. Before paying you should...
o: Hang up and call him back on his known number
Pay quickly, since it is family
Pay half first
qs.why: AI can copy voices. Calling back on a number you already have, or asking for the family code word, tells you the truth.

qs.q: What is a "family code word" for?
o: To confirm a caller really is your relative
To use as a password online
To unlock the phone
qs.why: Agree a secret word with family, and never type it into any website or app.

qs.q: A video of a famous person promises to double your money. What may it be?
o: A TV advert
A genuine offer
A deepfake, a fake video made with AI
qs.why: Fake celebrity endorsements are a favourite scam tool. Check the person's official channels.

qs.q: A WhatsApp message from a NEW number says, "Hi Mum, I lost my phone, send money to this account." First step?
o: Block your mum
Send the money
Call the old number or ask a question only they can answer
qs.why: Never pay before confirming. Pressure plus a new number is the pattern.

qs.q: How might scammers get your voice to copy?
o: They cannot copy voices
Only from phone calls
From short clips you post online or voice notes
qs.why: A few seconds of audio from public videos can be enough for AI tools, so think before posting.

bosses.name: Parcel Pete
bosses.tag: Holds your parcel to charge a fee
bosses.intro: Your parcel is stuck! Pay ₹49 on my link to release it!
bosses.beat: Parcel delivered. I lost the scam!

qs.q: "Your parcel is held. Pay ₹49 redelivery fee at this link." Smart move?
o: Reply with your card number
Pay ₹49, it is small
Do not use the link. Check tracking in the courier's official app or website
qs.why: A tiny fee is bait to get your card details or OTP.

qs.q: Which is typical of a fake courier message?
o: A tracking number you can check on the official site
A call after you placed an order
A link asking for card details or an OTP to pay a small fee
qs.why: Genuine couriers do not need your OTP or full card details to deliver.

qs.q: A "courier executive" says your parcel has illegal items and connects you to "police". You...
o: Obey the police officer
Hang up. This is how the digital arrest scam starts
Pay the fine
qs.why: Parcel plus police is a very common first step of that scam.

qs.q: You ordered nothing, but a "FedEx" caller says a parcel is in your name. What now?
o: Share your Aadhaar to verify
Pay the fee
Share nothing. Contact the courier through its official website
qs.why: Do not hand over IDs. Use contact details you find yourself.

qs.q: What is the safest way to track your orders?
o: A number a caller gave you
Links in SMS from unknown numbers
The shopping or courier app, or a website you typed yourself
qs.why: Official apps and typed addresses cannot be faked by a message.

bosses.name: Power-Cut Paul
bosses.intro: Pay your bill NOW or your electricity is cut tonight!
bosses.beat: Lights on! My threat fizzled out!

qs.q: An SMS says, "Your power will be cut at 9:30 pm unless you call 98xxxxxxxx and update your bill." You should...
o: Pay to that number
Call right away
Ignore the number and check your bill on the electricity board's official app or office
qs.why: A rush plus a mobile number is the pattern. Check only with the official board.

qs.q: Why do scammers send "disconnect tonight" messages?
o: To save electricity
To scare you into acting without thinking
To help you avoid a fine
qs.why: Fear and a deadline switch off careful thinking.

qs.q: The SMS asks you to install an "electricity bill app" file. What is wrong?
o: Apps from links can read your SMS and OTPs. Use only official stores
It may be slow
Nothing, it is fine
qs.why: A file sent in a message can steal your SMS and OTPs.

qs.q: Where can you safely pay your electricity bill?
o: A person on a phone call
A mobile number in an SMS
The board's official website or app, or a payment app after checking the biller
qs.why: Use the official channels you open yourself.

qs.q: You paid ₹10 to "update the meter" and now see unknown debits. First action?
o: Call 1930 and your bank straight away and block UPI and cards
Wait a few days
Pay more to fix it
qs.why: Speed matters. Call 1930, tell your bank and keep the proof.

bosses.name: Blackmail Bo
bosses.tag: Threatens to share your photos unless you pay
bosses.intro: Pay me or I will show everyone your photos! (I will keep asking forever.)
bosses.beat: Exposed! Blackmailers lose when you tell someone!

qs.q: Someone you met online threatens: "Pay ₹10,000 or I will post your photos." What should you do?
o: Pay to make it stop
Send more photos to prove it is you
Do not pay. Stop replying, save proof, tell a trusted adult and report to 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in
qs.why: Paying rarely ends it. Reporting early gives you the best protection, and adults you trust can help.

qs.q: Why does paying a blackmailer usually backfire?
o: They come back and ask for more
They stop for ever
They return the photos
qs.why: Once you pay, the criminal knows you will pay again.

qs.q: Should you delete the whole chat to hide it?
o: Yes, delete everything
No. Save screenshots, profile links, numbers and payment IDs as evidence
Delete it after a year
qs.why: Evidence helps the police find the person. Delete nothing before you report.

qs.q: If someone misuses a private photo of you, whose fault is it?
o: Only yours if you are under 18
Yours
The person blackmailing you. It is a crime and you deserve help
qs.why: Blackmail is the criminal's fault. Please tell a parent, teacher or another adult you trust.

qs.q: Who can help you if this happens?
o: Only the blackmailer
A parent, teacher or trusted adult, plus the 1930 helpline and cybercrime.gov.in
Nobody can help
qs.why: You are not alone. Telling someone is the first and strongest step.

generic.q: Unknown buyer · Chat: I will pay you ₹2,000 for the phone. Enter your UPI PIN on the request I sent so the money comes to you. What should you do?
o: Enter the PIN so the money arrives
Share the OTP you receive
Refuse, and check your own bank app for any credit
generic.why: A PIN is only for sending money. If you must enter one, money leaves your account.

generic.q: Shopkeeper · In person: You scan the QR printed on the shop counter. The app shows the shop's name and you enter your PIN to pay ₹180 for groceries. Is this safe?
o: No, never enter a PIN anywhere
Yes, you started the payment and the name matches the shop
No, shops must never use QR codes
generic.why: You chose to pay a known merchant and checked the name. Entering a PIN to pay is normal.

generic.q: +91 9•••••••• · Call: I am from your bank. Your KYC expires in 1 hour and your account will be blocked. Tell me the OTP that just came. What should you do?
o: Read out the OTP quickly
Hang up and call the number printed on your card
Ask the caller for their employee ID and then share
generic.why: Banks never ask for OTPs. Urgency is the trick. Always call back on an official number.

generic.q: Video call · Police uniform: A parcel in your name has drugs. You are under digital arrest. Stay on this call and do not tell your family. Pay ₹40,000 to clear the case. What should you do?
o: Stay on the call and pay to avoid arrest
Disconnect, tell your family and call 1930 if unsure
Negotiate a lower amount
generic.why: There is no digital arrest. Police never arrest on video call or ask for money to close a case.

generic.q: Bank app · Your own phone: You open your bank's official app yourself and see a button to update KYC. It asks you to upload your ID inside the app. Is this likely safe?
o: Probably yes: you opened the official app yourself
No, KYC can never be done in an app
No, you must do it at a cyber cafe
generic.why: You went to the official app on your own. Nobody pushed you or asked for an OTP over a call.

generic.q: Support agent · Phone call: Your refund is stuck. Please install AnyDesk and read me the 9-digit code so I can fix it from my side. What should you do?
o: Install it, since support needs to see the problem
Refuse and end the call
Install it but do not open your bank app
generic.why: Remote apps let a stranger control your phone and see your OTPs, even if you do not open your bank app.

generic.q: New number · WhatsApp: Hi, this is my new number. I lost my phone and I am in a hospital. Please send ₹8,000 urgently. Don't call. What should you do first?
o: Send a smaller amount to be safe
Call the person on their old saved number
Ask for a selfie and then pay
generic.why: Photos can be copied. Only a call to their old number, or someone who is with them, can confirm.

generic.q: Telegram group · Task job: You earned ₹300 for liking videos. To unlock your ₹4,000 withdrawal, deposit ₹2,000 as a task fee. What should you do?
o: Deposit once, because you have already earned money
Stop. Pay nothing and report the group
Ask friends to join to share the fee
generic.why: The small first payment builds trust. The deposits then grow and the money can never be withdrawn.

generic.q: SMS · Unknown sender: Your electricity will be cut tonight. Call officer Rao on 98XXXXXXXX and install the app to pay ₹10. What should you do?
o: Call and install the app to avoid disconnection
Check the bill in the official electricity board app or website
Forward it to 10 friends
generic.why: Boards do not disconnect over random SMS. The 'officer' wants control of your phone or payments.

generic.q: Friend next to you · In person: Your friend asks you to send ₹200 to his UPI ID for snacks. You can see him and the name on screen matches. Is this likely safe?
o: Yes, you know him and checked the name
No, never pay a friend by UPI
No, ask for his PIN first
generic.why: You know the person, can see them, and the payment is small and expected.

generic.q: What is India's national cyber crime helpline number?
generic.why: Call 1930 as soon as you notice a fraud. The first hour is the best chance to freeze the money.

generic.q: Where do you file an online complaint about cyber fraud?
o: uidai.gov.in
cybercrime.gov.in
incometax.gov.in
generic.why: The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal is cybercrime.gov.in. Keep the acknowledgement number.

generic.q: You lost money to a scammer 10 minutes ago. Best move?
o: Wait a day to see if it comes back
Post about it online first
Call 1930 and your bank right away
generic.why: Speed is everything when money must be frozen.

generic.q: What does your UPI PIN do?
o: Approves money leaving your account
Is shown to the sender
Lets you receive money
generic.why: A PIN only ever approves a payment or shows your balance.

generic.q: Which of these is fine to give a stranger who wants to pay you?
o: Your UPI PIN
Your UPI ID
The OTP you just got
generic.why: A UPI ID only lets people send you money.

generic.q: Where should you install apps from?
o: APK files from a friend
The official app store
Links in WhatsApp
generic.why: Files sent in chats can hide apps that read your SMS and OTPs.

generic.q: What protects your accounts best?
o: Different strong passwords plus 2-step login
One easy password everywhere
Sharing passwords with a friend as backup
generic.why: A unique password for each account plus a second step stops most account theft.

generic.q: A poster says "Scan to win an iPhone". What should you do?
o: Scan it and enter your PIN
Scan it quickly
Skip it. Never scan unknown QR codes for prizes
generic.why: Prize QR codes are bait. You cannot win a contest you did not enter.

generic.q: When is scanning a QR with your payment app normal?
o: When you chose to pay that shop or person and the name matches
When a stranger says you will receive money
When a caller asks you to verify KYC
generic.why: A scan is normal only when you decided to pay and checked the name.

generic.q: A caller says you must decide in 10 minutes. What does that tell you?
o: It is a polite reminder
It means the offer is rare and real
It is pressure, a classic scam sign
generic.why: Real banks and officials give you time and an official way to check.

tips: Receiving money never needs your PIN.
Banks never ask for your OTP, PIN or CVV.
Hang up and call the number on your card.
A deadline is a pressure trick. Slow down.
Never install AnyDesk or TeamViewer for a stranger.
No "digital arrest" exists in Indian law.
A padlock does not prove a site is honest.
Ask a family member before you pay in a hurry.
